Bobby Hull, known as The Golden Jet, was a Canadian left-winger and one of hockey's most electrifying scorers. His blazing speed, powerful slap shot, and blonde hair made him a cultural icon in the nineteen sixties and early nineteen seventies with the Chicago Blackhawks.

He scored six hundred ten goals and five hundred forty-nine assists for one thousand one hundred fifty-nine career points, which ranked third-most goals in NHL history at the time of his retirement. He was the first player to score fifty goals in a season in the modern era, which happened in nineteen sixty-one to sixty-two, shattering Maurice Richard's record of fifty goals in fifty games with fifty goals in eighty-four games instead.

Hull won the Hart Trophy for MVP twice and the Art Ross Trophy for leading scorer three times, establishing himself as an elite offensive force. He won the Stanley Cup with the Chicago Blackhawks in nineteen sixty-one and played on multiple Finals teams, and captained the Blackhawks for much of his career. He pioneered the modern slap shot with his physical strength and timing, making it a feared offensive weapon that future players would copy. In nineteen seventy-two, he jumped to the Winnipeg Jets of the WHA, the World Hockey Association, legitimizing the rival league and proving his marketability. He was known for his speed, toughness, and willingness to fight, wearing number nine and later number sixteen with the Jets.
